PAPER: Journal of Population Research (2026) 43:2 https://doi.org/10.1007/s12546-025-09410-0 ORIGINAL RESEARCH Unequal by age and household type: income inequality and demographic aging in Central and Eastern Europe Małgorzata Szczepaniak1 · Ewa Wędrowska1 · Joanna Muszyńska1 · Grzegorz Markowski1 Received: 4 June 2025 / Accepted: 25 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This study investigates the impact of demographic aging on income inequality in Central and Eastern European (CEE) states in 2005 and 2022. Using EU-SILC data, the analysis examines income disparities through the lenses of age and household type, exploring differences between CEE post-socialist liberal and corporatist wel- fare state typologies. The results highlight growing income disparities across age groups and household types, with elderly-headed households consistently recording lower incomes, particularly in the case of single-person elderly households, which may reflect the effects of demographic aging. Conversely, multi-generational house- holds mitigate inequality, offering more economic stability in both CEE liberal and corporatist states. The findings reveal significant variations between post-socialist welfare state typologies. Liberal post-socialist states, such as Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, exhibit higher overall inequality, whereas corporatist states, including Poland, Czechia, and Slovakia, demonstrate lower disparities. However, inequality among elderly households has risen in both typologies, with pronounced challenges in addressing the vulnerabilities of single-person elderly households. This study contributes to the neo-familial perspective, emphasizing the role of families and households in mitigating economic vulnerabilities, particularly in aging societies. The results underline the need for targeted policies, including strengthening redis- tributive pensions, incentivizing family caregiving, and supporting multi-genera- tional living arrangements to reduce inequalities exacerbated by demographic shifts. These insights inform policymakers seeking to balance demographic challenges with economic equity in rapidly aging societies. Introduction Concerns about population aging, driven by historically low fertility rates and increasing life expectancy, have been prominently observed in the European Union (EU) over recent decades (Fraccaroli & Deller, 2015). Population projections indi- cate that the aging of the EU’s population will accelerate in the future, with a rapid increase in the number and proportion of elderly individuals (65 years and older). The share of this demographic is projected to grow from 21% of the total population in EU-27 in 2022 to 30% by the mid-century in 2050 (European Commission, 2020). As Europe is the fastest-aging region globally, both EU member states and the Euro- pean Commission have prioritized innovative and sustainable policies for the elderly population (Yenilmez, 2015). Moreover, initiatives targeting older adults align with twelve distinct Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) being the most frequently discussed in the literature (Shevelkova et al., 2023). Central and Eastern European (CEE) states present a compelling case in this context (Dorjnyambuu, 2024). These states share historical parallels related to sys- temic transformations undertaken since the collapse of communist regimes in the late 1980 s (Cook & Inglot, 2021). Notably, they are experiencing a faster and more pronounced aging of their populations. At the onset of these systemic changes, CEE societies were relatively young, with median ages ranging from 31 years in Slovakia to 36 years in Hungary. By the time of EU accession in 2004, median ages had risen across all CEE states, reaching approximately 39 years in most of the region, except for Slovakia and Poland, which remained the youngest. By 2022, the median age in CEE states had approached the EU-27 average of 44 years, ranging from 43 years in Slovakia to 45 years in Lithuania. Projections suggest that by mid-century, the median age in CEE states will exceed the EU-27 average, rising to 49 years compared to 48 years for the EU-27 (Eurostat, 2020). The accelerated aging in CEE states is further reflected by the increasing share of the elderly (65+). Countries such as Lithuania, Latvia, and Poland are projected to see over 30% of their populations in this age group by 2050, surpassing the EU-27 average of 30% (Eurostat, 2020). This demographic shift is exacerbated by popu- lation declines in CEE states, contrasting with a projected increase in the overall EU-27 population, thereby intensifying the challenges faced by the region. The old- age dependency ratio (OADR) highlights this demographic transition, particularly in Poland and the Baltic states, which have shifted from being among the youngest to the oldest countries demographically. Differences in the dynamics of population aging across Europe stem from variations in the timing of the second demographic transition, which began approximately two decades later in CEE states (Kiniorska et al., 2023). Among CEE states, Lithuania, Latvia, and Poland are experiencing par- ticularly rapid aging due to declining fertility rates and outward migration of younger workers. Hoff (2008) posits that population aging in CEE is an unintended consequence of the socio-economic transition from communist to capitalist systems. The aging processes in these states are not only characterized by an unprecedented increase in 1 3 Unequal by age and household type: income inequality and… Page 3 of 34 2 the elderly population but are compounded by significant emigration of young people and improvements in life expectancy. According to United Nations projections, nine of the ten fastest-shrinking countries globally are in Eastern Europe, a trend with profound implications for economic growth and the European prosperity envisioned after the fall of communism (Petrakis, 2020). CEE states, which transitioned from communist regimes to democracies and mar- ket economies, have also witnessed rising income inequality since the late 1980 s (Milanovic, 1999; Mitra & Yemtsov, 2006; World Bank, 1996). In the early years of systemic transformation, income inequality levels in CEE were comparable to those in many Western European countries (World Bank, 1996). However, significant variations in inequality emerged by the 1990 s and after EU accession. In 1993, Baltic countries exhibited substantially higher income inequality compared to Poland, Slo- vakia, Czechia, and Hungary. By the time of EU accession in 2004, some CEE states, such as Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, maintained above-average inequality levels, while others, such as Slovakia and Czechia, had some of the lowest inequality levels in both CEE and the EU. By 2022, nearly two decades of EU membership had contributed to a reduction in income inequality across all CEE states. The observed variations in inequality are attributable to differences in institutional legacies and transition policies. These factors are often considered in regime classifi- cations. Given the shared trajectory of post-communist transformation, CEE states are frequently classified as post-socialist welfare states in regard to Esping-Andersen’s (1990) typology (Eurofound, 2014; Whelan & Maitre, 2010). These states emphasize equality of living conditions and prefer government intervention to achieve these goals (Cook & Inglot, 2021; Min & Ko, 2022). However, distinctions in income inequality have led to the categorization of CEE states into two groups: CEE liberal (North) and CEE corporatist (Continental) welfare states (Eurofound, 2014; Gallie & Paugam, 2000; Whelan, 2010; World Bank, 2018). The former, exemplified by Lat- via, Lithuania, and Estonia, is characterized by high income inequality and flexible labor markets, while the latter, including Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia, and Poland, features lower income inequality and transfer-oriented labor markets with moderate employment protection (Eurofound, 2014; Gallie & Paugam, 2000). Despite extensive research on rising income inequality in CEE post-communism (Dorjnyambuu, 2024; World Bank, 1996), most discussions have focused on eco- nomic dimensions, such as wage disparities (Magda et al., 2021; Śliwicki & Rycz- kowski, 2014; Večerník, 2012), income inequality (Brzeziński, 2018; Bukowski et al., 2023, 2024; Bukowski & Novokmet, 2021; Večerník, 2012), and wealth inequal- ity (Brzezinski & Sałach, 2021). However, limited attention has been paid to demo- graphic factors, such as aging and household transformations, and their relationship to income inequality. Furthermore, the connection between aging processes and income inequality, considering differences in welfare state classifications, remains underexplored. Given the sensitivity of inequality to demographic change (European Commis- sion, 2013; Rechel et al., 2013), and the particularly rapid aging of CEE societies (Bražinová & Chytil, 2024; WHO, 2011), it is essential to examine how age and fam- ily structures shape economic disparities in this region. Incorporating age and house- hold type as determinants of inequality enables a nuanced understanding of these 1 3 2 Page 4 of 34 M. Szczepaniak et al. processes (Foster & Lokshin, 2024; Sen, 2001). Household composition influences access to pooled resources and exposure to poverty risks, with single-person and single-parent households being especially vulnerable in post-socialist contexts with weaker redistributive welfare systems (Muszyńska & Wędrowska, 2020; Medgyesi, 2014). The designation of household headship adds further complexity (Kleinjans, 2013). In CEE countries, headship has historically been linked to patriarchy and patrilineal traditions, with the oldest male typically recognized as the head, while female-headed households often arise from absence, widowhood, or migration and face higher risks of poverty (Szołtysek, 2012). Despite modernization and rising diversity in household forms, these cultural norms continue to shape resource distri- bution and economic vulnerability. In this context, elderly-headed and single-person elderly households remain particularly disadvantaged, whereas multi-generational households often mitigate risks through shared resources (Botev, 2012). Consider- ing both age effects and household structures therefore provides a richer framework for understanding how demographic and familial changes interact with inequality in post-communist societies. Given these trends, this article examines how income disparities across age groups and household types have evolved in CEE, offering insights into how these patterns reflect age effects in shaping inequality. Specifically, it seeks to:: 1. Evaluate demographic trends in aging within the CEE region and their implica- tions for income inequality. 2. Identify the types of households in which elderly individuals reside. 3. Assess the degree of inequality across the general population and distinct age subgroups. 4. Evaluate the impact of the household head’s age on equivalized income inequal- ity in CEE states. 5. Investigate the role of household type, particularly those membered by the elderly, in shaping equivalized income inequality in CEE states. 6. Provide policy recommendations to address income disparities exacerbated by aging populations. This study contributes to the literature in two significant ways. First, it examines the impact of age on income inequality to improve our understanding of how popula- tion aging interacts with economic disparities in post-communist states. The analysis incorporates the diversity in income inequality observed after CEE states’ accession to the EU, distinguishing between two clusters of post-socialist welfare states: CEE liberal and CEE corporatist. While previous studies have applied these classifications to examine systemic and economic differences (Eurofound, 2014; World Bank, 2018), life satisfaction (Whelan, 2010), and relationships between income inequalities and well-being dimensions (Geise & Szczepaniak, 2025), no research has explored aging in relation to income inequality from this perspective within CEE states. Further- more, the sustainability of financial protection systems in the context of population aging emerges as a critical issue for welfare states. Second, by analyzing equivalized household income, this study incorporates both the economic and social functions of families and households. These functions are evolving in response to population aging, making it crucial to identify how these changes affect income distribution. The methodological approach - a decomposition of income inequality (“a priori approach”) based on household-level rather than indi- vidual-level data - underscores the household’s role in mitigating the economic vul- nerability of the elderly, a demographic group experiencing unprecedented growth in CEE states. Historically, families have served as the primary support system for meeting the needs of dependent elderly individuals (WHO, 2011). However, as the aging process transforms family dynamics, there is an urgent need to develop family policy recommendations tailored to these changes. In particular, it is important to recognize that family policies in CEE states have traditionally focused on children rather than the elderly (Cook & Inglot, 2021). In a broader context, this study engages with the concept of neo-familism, which examines the evolving role of families and households in supporting elderly individuals (Bražinová & Chytil, 2024; Yan, 2018). This approach provides a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by elderly families/households in rapidly aging societies, particularly within CEE states. The study’s findings inform the development of age-adjusted family and household poli- cies that promote the financial security of the elderly, protect them from poverty, and reduce their vulnerability, thereby contributing to societal sustainability. Theoretical background Population aging is widely recognized as a significant factor contributing to income inequality. Scholars have long argued that as populations age, income distribution becomes increasingly uneven (Drosdowski et al., 2015; Hwang et al., 2021). Research shows that inequality within age cohorts tends to grow as individuals age, with popu- lation aging cited as a driver of rising overall inequality (Deaton & Paxson, 1994; Crystal et al., 2017; Hungerford, 2020). Dolls et al. (2018) project that demographic shifts will exacerbate inequality, as income tends to be distributed more unevenly among older cohorts than younger ones. Hwang et al. (2021) highlight that a rising proportion of retirees reduces average household income and intensifies inequality. CEE states face unique challenges in this context, as their populations are aging more rapidly than those in Western Europe. Rapid demographic shifts in CEE states contribute to labor shortages, which, in turn, increase income disparities. These chal- lenges are compounded by population decline and a growing number of retirees, further exacerbating income inequality (Petrakis, 2020). Despite these urgent issues, the relationship between population aging and income inequality in CEE states has been relatively underexplored in the literature. Post-socialist welfare systems in CEE states are particularly vulnerable to the twin pressures of aging populations and rising income inequality. Since the 1990 s, demographic trends in these countries have included sharp declines in fertility rates, delayed childbearing and marriage, and shrinking populations. These trends pose sig- nificant challenges to the sustainability of social systems (Brainerd, 2010). While tax-benefit systems in many countries are effective in moderating income inequality caused by demographic changes (Dolls et al., 2018), the more rapid aging processes in CEE states create acute pressures on pension systems. Research indicates that the design of pension systems plays a critical role in shaping the impact of aging on income inequality. For instance, countries with less redistributive pension systems, such as the Baltic states, show higher levels of poverty and inequality among older populations compared to countries with robust systems, like the Nordic states (Ebb- inghaus, 2021; Filauro et al., 2023). Inadequate pension provisions further exacerbate disparities, particularly among vulnerable groups, such as women and lower-income individuals. In addition to natural population decline, significant emigration of younger, working-age individuals from CEE states accelerates demographic aging. This trend reduces the pool of potential caregivers and contributors to social security systems, straining resources for elderly support (Botev, 2012). The outmigration of younger populations not only intensifies the aging process but also undermines intergenera- tional support systems, which are critical for mitigating income inequality. Older generations in CEE states are disproportionately affected by these demographic shifts, experiencing greater poverty and social exclusion due to their limited ability to adapt to economic and political transformations (Botev, 2012). Population aging is also associated with shifts in household composition, includ- ing a growing number of single-person households among older individuals. Smaller households often face higher risks of poverty because they lack the economies of scale that benefit larger households (Filauro et al., 2023). Additionally, older adults 1 3 Unequal by age and household type: income inequality and… Page 7 of 34 2 living alone frequently experience reduced social support and increased feelings of loneliness (Bražinová & Chytil, 2024; Yeh & Lo, 2004). These changes in house- hold structures influence income distribution and contribute to broader patterns of inequality. The role of households/families further complicates the relationship between demographic shifts and income inequality. Households play multiple roles in the economy (Bagautdinova et al., 2014): they generate and accumulate income, con- sume goods and services, save and invest, and pay taxes. Moreover, households are integral to the functioning of social systems, as they create, develop, and sustain human capabilities. Households collect and redistribute income among their mem- bers, creating economies of scale and offering partial protection against temporary income losses or other shocks. In this role, they serve as vital “social safety provid- ers” (Muszyńska & Wędrowska, 2023). They contribute significantly to human well- being by meeting basic needs daily while also fulfilling essential social roles. This study draws on Katz’s definition of social reproduction, which includes the biological reproduction of human life through both every day and intergenerational activities and practices, and the production and reproduction of a socially differentiated labor force (Katz, 2002). Santos and Tertilt (2024) emphasize, however, that household structure can function not only as a mitigator of economic inequality but also as an amplifier. This is because, over time and across generations, families are responsible for most of the human capital investment in the next generation, which can perpetuate income disparities over time. In CEE states, declining fertility rates and assortative mating, where individuals marry within similar income or education groups, widen income gaps between household types (Muszyńska & Wędrowska, 2020). Further- more, earlier childbearing in the region has resulted in shorter generational intervals, potentially affecting caregiving arrangements and intergenerational income inequal- ity (Botev, 2012). Changes in household structures, such as an increase in single-person households among older individuals, have additional implications for income inequality. Smaller households often face higher poverty risks due to the absence of shared economic resources (Filauro et al., 2023). At the same time, social dynamics within households influence income redistribution. Families act as buffers against economic shocks but can also serve to reproduce existing inequalities, depending on household composi- tion and intergenerational dynamics (Almås et al., 2021; Bražinová & Chytil, 2024; Kiernan et al., 2024). For example, inequalities across households influence family formation and dissolution, which can have long-term effects on income distribution (Muszyńska & Wędrowska, 2020; Blossfeld & Buchholz, 2009; Grotti & Scherer, 2016). Moreover, the concept of household headship is relevant for analyzing inequality, since empirical studies often classify households by the age or gender of the head. Yet, headship is a socially constructed category that may obscure intra-household dynamics, as the designated head is not always the main decision-maker or income provider (Kleinjans, 2013). In CEE states, where rapid demographic shifts have intersected with post-transition family transformations, elderly-headed and female- headed households are disproportionately vulnerable, while multi-generational 1 3 2 Page 8 of 34 M. Szczepaniak et al. households may alleviate risks through shared resources (Botev, 2012; Muszyńska & Wędrowska, 2018, 2020). As the population ages, the interplay between household structure and income inequality becomes increasingly critical. Pension systems, while vital for reducing poverty among older populations, often replicate income inequalities established during working life, particularly in systems with limited redistributive mechanisms (Ebbinghaus, 2021). Social policies aimed at addressing inequality must account for the dual role of families and households in mitigating and perpetuating disparities, especially as household dynamics evolve in response to demographic shifts. To assess the contribution of differences in average income between groups to the overall levels of income inequality in the countries studied, we perform a decompo- sition of income inequality. The two main approaches to inequality decomposition analysis can be broadly categorized as “a priori approaches” and “regression mod- els” (Cowell & Fiorio, 2011). A priori approach is perhaps most familiar in terms of inequality decomposition by population subgroups (Shorrocks, 1980, 1984; Foster & Shneyerov, 1999; Deutsch & Silber, 1999; Ogwang, 2014). The second analytical strand of inequality-decomposition analysis (regression models) was used by Fields and Yoo (2000), Bourguignon et al. (2008), Hwang et al. (2021). In this article, we employ the standard decomposition technique (“a priori approach”), which requires: (1) partitioning the population into mutually exclusive and exhaustive subsets, (2) defining a representative income for each group, and (3) selecting an inequality measure that satisfies the property of additive decomposition. Moreover, “a priori approach” is based on the appropriate axiomatization of inequal- ity measures. The fact that income inequality has far-reaching social implications makes the methods used to measure it critically important. The most accepted criterion for clas- sifying inequality indices is their relationship to the concept of social evaluation. Based on this criterion, inequality measures can be divided into two broad classes: normative and positive. Normative measures are grounded in an ethical framework linked to social welfare functions (SWF), as developed by Kolm (1969), Atkinson (1970), and Sen (1973), and are therefore shaped by value judgments. In the norma- tive approach, inequality measures are derived from SWF, which incorporates explicit value judgments about distributive justice through well-defined axioms (Bosmans et al., 2015). This provides the resulting inequality measures with a normative founda- tion. When social welfare is evaluated using a conventional SWF, inequality is inter- preted as a loss of welfare (Villar, 2017). Positive analysis does not explicitly use the concept of social welfare. Positive inequality measures primarily serve a descriptive role, suitably conveying the degree of inequality in an appropriate way and explor- ing the causes and consequences of inequality. However, Sen (1973) notes that this distinction is not precise since even positive measures of inequality are inherently linked to SWF (e.g., the Theil index). The selection of a measure for assessing income inequality should align with the objectives of the study. Given that positive measures help one to assess the signif- icance of the impact of various factors (e.g. age, household type) on the level of inequality, we opted to use such a measure in our analysis. However, in most of the countries studied, this impact has declined by 2022. 1 3 Unequal by age and household type: income inequality and… Page 27 of 34 2 Discussion and conclusions This article provides a comprehensive analysis of income disparities across age groups and household types and their economic impacts on income distribution, dem- onstrating the critical role of age and household type in driving income inequality across CEE states and addressing the links between population aging and income inequalities. It is important to note that the analysis captures age-related income dif- ferences at specific points in time, rather than the dynamic effects of demographic aging. Therefore, while these differences may align with broader aging trends, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence that demographic aging directly causes increased inequality. The results of our study are in line with Dolls et al. (2018), Deaton and Paxson (1994), Crystal et al., (2017), Hungerford (2020), and Hwang et al. (2021). However, it highlights how income disparities evolved between 2005 and 2022, focusing on the vulnerability of elderly households in two post-socialist wel- fare state typologies, i.e. post-socialist corporatist and liberal. The findings emphasize the increasing influence of demographic aging and household structures on economic outcomes, with significant implications for policy design and neo-familism. The analysis shows that age significantly shapes income inequality, with older households -particularly those led by individuals aged 65 and over - consistently recording lower incomes and higher inequality. In 2005, the decomposition of income inequality by the age of the household head revealed a moderate effect of age on inequality, with the highest level observed in Czechia (5.1%). By 2022, most countries experienced a significant increase in this effect, reaching as high impact as 10.3% in Estonia. This reflects the rapid aging processes in CEE states and their profound impact on income distribution. Older people aged 65 and over most often live in single-person or couple households. By 2022, the share of elderly individuals living alone increased in Czechia, Estonia, and Lithuania, while in other countries, the proportion of older people in extended and multi-generational households grew. Living in a multi-generational household is often driven by necessity, influenced by income levels or care needs. These findings underscore how aging amplifies income disparities and highlights the economic vulnerability of elderly households. Household type plays a critical role in shaping income inequality. Single-person elderly households are particularly vulnerable, consistently showing the lowest equiv- alized incomes per household member, with the lack of the economies of scale that benefit larger households, leaving them exposed to poverty and economic insecurity. Conversely, multi-generational households mitigate the economic effects of aging through shared support systems and resource pooling, buffering against inequality. This aligns with previous studies that highlight the stabilizing role of extended fam- ily structures (Bražinová & Chytil, 2024; Filauro et al., 2023). The decomposition analysis revealed that household type had a significant impact on inequality levels in 2005, with the highest effect observed in Czechia (29.4%). However, by 2022, this impact declined in most CEE countries, reflecting shifts in household structures and economic dynamics. The study highlights significant differences in income inequality trends between liberal and corporatist post-socialist welfare states that align with the former classifi- cation of Eurofound (2014), World Bank (2018), and Whelan and Maitre ((Whelan, 1 3 2 Page 28 of 34 M. Szczepaniak et al. and Maître, 2010)) but extending the analysis regarding aging and household type on income inequalities. In liberal post-socialist states (Baltic countries), older house- holds, particularly single-person ones, face pronounced income inequality due to less redistributive social protection systems. For example, Lithuania and Estonia recorded significantly widening income disparities for the elderly between 2005 and 2022. In contrast, corporatist welfare states (e.g., Czechia, Slovakia, and Poland) demonstrate relatively lower inequality levels among elderly households, supported by more robust social security systems. Multi-generational households in these states exhibit greater economic stability, with lower inequality and higher incomes, under- scoring their role in mitigating disparities. However, some corporatist states, such as Hungary, showed a significant increase in inequality among the oldest households. Based on these findings, tailored policy interventions are essential to address income inequality among the elderly. For liberal welfare states, strengthening redis- tributive mechanisms in pension systems to reduce income disparities is crucial. Targeted subsidies for single elderly individuals, particularly for housing and living costs, would alleviate economic vulnerabilities. Additionally, introducing tax credits for families providing housing and care for elderly relatives could foster intergen- erational support. For corporatist welfare states, enhancing family-centric policies through tax breaks and incentives for families supporting elderly relatives would reduce dependency on public welfare systems. Expanding support systems for multi- generational households would sustain their stabilizing role in income inequality in all the CEE states studied. While the association between household composition and income inequality is evident in our findings, these relationships should not be inter- preted as causal without further longitudinal or quasi-experimental analysis. Across CEE states, single-person households face the lowest incomes and high- est relative inequality, reflecting the vulnerability of elderly individuals living alone (Yeh & Lo, 2004). The importance of family and household-based social security is evident in the higher incomes and lower inequality observed in extended and multi- generational households. However, differences in how age and household type affect income inequalities between liberal and corporatist states underscore the critical role of welfare state classifications, even in the group of the post-socialist CEE states with the historical similarities of systemic transformation after the demise of the com- munist rule (Cook & Inglot, 2021). Policymakers must consider these distinctions to develop effective strategies for reducing disparities and ensuring economic security for aging populations. This article contributes to the neo-familial perspective by analyzing the evolving role of families and households in mitigating economic vulnerabilities but addressing it to CEE states, which broadens the approach of Yan (2018). The findings demon- strate that extended and multi-generational households play a critical role in buffer- ing economic challenges, particularly for elderly individuals in states with weaker social security systems. This aligns with neo-familism’s emphasis on the family as an essential unit of social and economic support, especially in post-socialist contexts. Families adapt to compensate for structural weaknesses, fostering intergenerational dependency and cooperation to promote economic security, which is particularly important in rapidly aging CEE states. Policies that support diverse household struc- tures, including multi-generational living, may help mitigate income disparities—but 1 3 Unequal by age and household type: income inequality and… Page 29 of 34 2 should be evaluated carefully given the potential trade-offs and the absence of causal evidence in this study. JSON: Name: age_household_inequality_cee Title: Decomposing changes in equivalized household income inequality by age and household type in Central and Eastern Europe using generalized entropy decomposition and counterfactual reweighting Short Hypothesis: Between 2005 and 2022, changes in population shares of households headed by persons aged 65+ causally increased the between-group component of equivalized household disposable income inequality in the seven studied CEE countries. Related Work: Existing approaches to measuring the contribution of demographic structure to income inequality fall into two main strands: (1) a priori subgroup decompositions (generalized entropy / Theil class) that partition total inequality into within- and between-group components, and (2) regression-based decompositions that attribute variance to covariates via earnings or income regressions. Prior studies of aging and inequality typically apply these decompositions at the individual level or focus on pension systems, while research on household effects emphasizes household type or head characteristics but rarely integrates both age and household composition across multiple countries. Limitations of prior work include: inconsistent use of equivalence scales, sparse treatment of survey vs register data measurement error (top incomes and under-reporting), limited inference (few studies report bootstrap SEs or tests for decomposition shares), inadequate sensitivity analyses (equivalence scales, headship rules, top-income trimming), and scarce cross-country comparative work across welfare typologies that isolates the joint effect of age and household type. Causal claims are rarely supported by counterfactual reweighting or simulation, leaving unresolved whether observed demographic shifts can explain changes in between-group inequality. Abstract: This project quantifies how demographic aging and household composition jointly contributed to changes in equivalized household disposable income inequality in seven Central and Eastern European countries between 2005 and 2022. Using EU-SILC microdata, we compute generalized entropy (GE) measures (α = -1, 0, 1, 2) of equivalized household income and apply additive subgroup decomposition to separate within- and between-group inequality by (a) age of household head and (b) elderly household type (single, couple, extended, multigenerational). We complement the a priori decomposition with counterfactual reweighting and regression-based decompositions to estimate the effect of changing population shares on inequality, and use bootstrap inference for statistical significance. The main contribution is a robust, multi-method quantification of the portion of inequality change attributable to aging-driven compositional shifts and household structure, and a comparative assessment across liberal and corporatist post-socialist welfare typologies. Expected outcomes include precise estimates of between-group share changes, sensitivity profiles to scale and headship choices, and policy-relevant diagnostics for pension and family-support interventions. Experiments: Datasets: EU-SILC cross-sectional UDB 2023 microdata for years 2005 and 2022 restricted to Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia; variables: household disposable income (gross minus taxes/transfers), equivalized income per person (OECD-modified scale), household head age, household composition flags, pension income component, person and household weights, sample identifiers. Preprocessing: apply cross-sectional weights, remove observations with missing income or core composition variables, generate household-type categories (single, couple, extended without children, multigenerational with children), construct alternative equivalized incomes (per-capita, square-root scale) for ablation. Baselines: (A) Standard GE decomposition (α = -1,0,1,2) by age-head groups and by elderly household type; (B) Individual-level GE decomposition for comparison; (C) Regression-based decomposition (Fields/Bourguignon style) using log equivalized income regressed on age, household type, education, employment status; (D) Oaxaca–Blinder style mean decomposition. Proposed analyses: 1) Compute total GE(1) (Theil) and within-/between-group components for each country and year for both partitionings (age-head; elderly household type). 2) Counterfactual reweighting: hold 2005 within-group distributions constant and reweight subgroup population shares to 2022; compute counterfactual total inequality and attribute change to compositional shift. 3) Statistical inference: bootstrap household-level resampling with 1,000 replications to estimate standard errors and 95% CIs for GE totals and between-group share differences; conduct paired permutation tests for change significance. 4) Ablation studies: (i) alternative equivalence scales (OECD-modified vs per-capita vs square-root), (ii) alternative headship rules (oldest male preference vs self-reported head), (iii) exclusion of pension income from household income, (iv) top-income trimming and top-correction (trim top 1% and compare), (v) country-group comparisons (liberal vs corporatist). 5) Robustness: repeat decompositions using GE(α) for α = -1,0,1,2 and report sensitivity. Evaluation metrics: GE(α) values, between-group share (% between/total), change in between-group share 2005→2022, bootstrap SE and p-values, regression R2 and explained share attributable to age/household type. Deliverables: tabulated country-year decompositions, counterfactual attribution fractions, ablation sensitivity matrix, and statistical significance summaries. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Data measurement: EU-SILC heterogeneity (survey vs register-based income collection) and under-reporting of top incomes can bias GE measures, especially GE(2) and GE(-1); top-correction approaches are imperfect. 2) Headship and composition coding errors: socially constructed head definitions and misreporting can misclassify age-of-head and household-type categories, altering subgroup shares. 3) Causal inference limits: decomposition and reweighting establish attribution to compositional change but cannot fully establish causality because of unobserved confounding and simultaneous policy or labor-market changes. 4) Small subgroup samples: rare household types or small elderly subgroups in some countries yield high variance and low power for bootstrap inference. 5) Sensitivity to assumptions: results depend on equivalence scale, GE parameter α, and treatment of pension income; conclusions may vary across reasonable choices. 6) Projection/scaling limits: counterfactual reweighting projects past composition to present but ignores behavioral responses and endogenous income adjustments, limiting external validity to other periods or policy scenarios. 7) Computation and reproducibility: bootstrap and multiple ablations require moderate compute; reproducibility depends on access to microdata and exact weighting procedures.
